Standard Text: Analyze the growth of Middle Tennessee in the early 1800s in power and influence, including the relocation of the capital.
What the Chart Shows: Line chart showing Tennessee's total population rising each decade from the first federal census in 1790 through 1860.
Data Source: U.S. Decennial Census, total resident population of Tennessee, 1790-1860 (Campbell Gibson & Kay Jung, 'Historical Census Statistics on Population Totals')
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Census Bureau, Historical Census Statistics on Population Totals by Race, 1790-1990, and by Hispanic Origin, 1970-1990, for the United States, Regions, Divisions, and States (Working Paper No. 56).
Build Note: Supports the 'coming of age' theme and the rise of Middle Tennessee's influence; teachers can pair with the decade-by-decade shift of population weight toward the Middle Grand Division (which drove the capital's relocation to Nashville).

Standard Text: Describe the distribution of slaves between the three grand divisions of Tennessee, the lives of free blacks and slaves, and the role of Tennesseans in the early abolition movement (e.g., Elihu Embree).
Chart Title: Enslaved and Free Black Population of Tennessee, 1790-1820
What the Chart Shows: Grouped bar chart comparing the number of enslaved people and free Black Tennesseans at each early census from 1790 through 1820.
Data Source: U.S. Decennial Census population schedules for Tennessee (Southwest Territory 1790/95, then 1800, 1810, 1820), counts of enslaved persons and free persons of color
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Census Bureau, Return of the Whole Number of Persons... (First through Fourth Censuses, 1790-1820), Tennessee tables.
Build Note: Illustrates the small early free-Black population against a rapidly growing enslaved population; pairs with the standard's focus on the lives of free Blacks and enslaved people and the early abolition movement.

Standard Text: Describe the significance of the Mississippi River, the Jackson Purchase, and the introduction of cotton in the rapid growth of Memphis and West Tennessee.
Chart Title: The Rise of Memphis: Population Growth, 1820-1900
What the Chart Shows: Line chart tracing Memphis's steep population climb from a small river town in 1820 to a major city by 1900.
Data Source: U.S. Census Bureau population of the 100 largest urban places / decennial census municipal population for Memphis, TN, 1820-1900
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: Campbell Gibson, Population of the 100 Largest Cities and Other Urban Places in the United States: 1790 to 1990 (U.S. Census Bureau Working Paper No. 27, 1998).
Build Note: Connects the Jackson Purchase, the Mississippi River, and the cotton trade to Memphis's explosive growth; the visible dip/plateau around 1880 also foreshadows the yellow fever epidemic (TN.41).

Standard Text: Explain the importance of transportation, technology, and geography in Tennessee’s growing involvement in the national economy after the War of 1812, including the significance of: Cash crops (e.g., cotton, tobacco); Natchez Trace; Road improvements; Steamboats
Chart Title: Tennessee Cash Crops: Cotton and Tobacco Production, 1840-1860
What the Chart Shows: Grouped bar chart comparing Tennessee's cotton and tobacco output across the 1840, 1850, and 1860 agricultural censuses.
Data Source: U.S. Census of Agriculture, Tennessee cotton (bales) and tobacco (pounds) output, 1840, 1850, 1860
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Census Office, Agriculture of the United States in 1860 (and 1850, 1840 census compendia), Tennessee state tables.
Build Note: Directly supports the standard's cash-crop focus and shows how improved transportation (steamboats, roads, the Natchez Trace) fed rising commodity output before the Civil War.

Standard Text: Describe the development of slavery in Tennessee from 1800 to 1860, including the distribution of slaves and conflicting attitudes among the three grand divisions.
Chart Title: Growth of Slavery in Tennessee: Enslaved Population by Decade, 1800-1860
What the Chart Shows: Area chart showing the steady rise in Tennessee's enslaved population from 1800 through its peak in 1860.
Data Source: U.S. Decennial Census, enslaved population of Tennessee, 1800-1860
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Census Office, Population of the United States in 1860 (and prior decennial compendia), Tennessee slave population tables.
Build Note: Core to the standard's focus on 'the development of slavery in Tennessee from 1800 to 1860'; the sharp climb ties to cotton expansion in West Tennessee.

Standard Text: Explain the causes of the Civil War and how geographic and political divisions impacted Tennessee’s secession.
Chart Title: Enslaved Share of Population by Grand Division, 1860
What the Chart Shows: Bar chart comparing the enslaved population as a percentage of total population in East, Middle, and West Tennessee in 1860.
Data Source: U.S. 1860 Census county-level population, aggregated to East, Middle, and West Tennessee grand divisions (enslaved persons as a share of total population)
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Census Office, Population of the United States in 1860, Tennessee county tables (grouped by grand division).
Build Note: Explains the geographic-political divide behind Tennessee's secession vote: Unionist East Tennessee had few enslaved people, while cotton-heavy West Tennessee had a high enslaved share. Requires grouping counties by division.

Standard Text: Describe Tennessee’s role in the Civil War, including: Sieges of Fort Henry and Fort Donelson; Battle of Shiloh; Battle of Stones River; Chattanooga Campaign; Johnsonville Campaign; Battle of Franklin; Battle of Nashville
Chart Title: Major Civil War Engagements in Tennessee by Year, 1861-1865
What the Chart Shows: Bar chart showing the number of significant Civil War engagements fought in Tennessee in each year from 1861 to 1865.
Data Source: NPS Civil War Sites Advisory Commission (CWSAC) battle summaries, engagements located in Tennessee, counted by year
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program, CWSAC Report on the Nation's Civil War Battlefields, Tennessee battle summaries.
Build Note: Quantifies why Tennessee saw more Civil War fighting than almost any state except Virginia; the standard lists specific battles (Fort Donelson, Shiloh, Stones River, Franklin, Nashville) that can be mapped to the yearly counts.

Standard Text: Describe how the Civil War impacted various populations in Tennessee (e.g., African Americans, American Indians, and women).
What the Chart Shows: Grouped bar chart comparing Tennessee's white and Black populations in 1860 and 1870, before and after emancipation.
Data Source: U.S. Decennial Census, Tennessee population by race (white and Black/'colored'), 1860 and 1870
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Census Office, The Statistics of the Population of the United States (Ninth Census, 1870), Tennessee tables; Population of the United States in 1860.
Build Note: The 1870 census is the first to count formerly enslaved people as free citizens; comparing 1860 and 1870 shows the demographic transformation the Civil War brought to Tennessee's African American population.

Standard Text: Explain developments in Tennessee’s farming during the late 19th century as a result of industrialization.
Chart Title: Tennessee Farms after the Civil War: Number of Farms and Average Size, 1860-1900
What the Chart Shows: Combination chart showing Tennessee's rising number of farms alongside falling average farm size from 1860 to 1900.
Data Source: U.S. Census of Agriculture, Tennessee number of farms and average farm acreage, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1890, 1900
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Census Office, Census of Agriculture reports for Tennessee, 1860-1900.
Build Note: The rising farm count with shrinking average size documents the spread of sharecropping and tenant farming after the war, central to New South farming developments.

Standard Text: Explain developments in Tennessee’s farming during the late 19th century as a result of industrialization.
Chart Title: Railroad Expansion in Tennessee: Track Mileage, 1850-1900
What the Chart Shows: Line chart showing the growth of railroad track mileage in Tennessee from mid-century through 1900.
Data Source: Historical Statistics of the United States, railroad mileage operated (state/regional series), with Census railroad statistics for Tennessee, 1850-1900
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Census Bureau, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (Bicentennial Edition, 1975), railroad mileage series.
Build Note: Railroad expansion is the engine of New South industrialization that reshaped Tennessee farming and connected interior counties to markets.

Standard Text: Discuss the impact of the yellow fever epidemic on Memphis.
Chart Title: Memphis Population Collapse During the Yellow Fever Era, 1870-1880
What the Chart Shows: Line chart showing Memphis's population before and after the 1878 yellow fever epidemic, highlighting the sharp mid-decade decline.
Data Source: U.S. Census Bureau municipal population for Memphis, 1870 and 1880 (bracketing the 1878 yellow fever epidemic)
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: Campbell Gibson, Population of the 100 Largest Cities... 1790 to 1990 (U.S. Census Bureau Working Paper No. 27, 1998); Population of the United States, Ninth and Tenth Censuses.
Build Note: The census shows Memphis's population barely growing (or falling) across the 1870s despite prior boom growth, quantifying the epidemic's demographic devastation and the exodus it triggered.

Standard Text: Describe the events that led to the Coal Creek Wars in Anderson and the surrounding counties over the state of Tennessee’s decision to replace coal miners with prisoners.
What the Chart Shows: Line chart showing rising annual coal production in Tennessee through the 1880s and 1890s.
Data Source: USGS Mineral Resources of the United States, annual Tennessee coal output (short tons), 1880s-1900
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Geological Survey, Mineral Resources of the United States (annual volumes), coal production by state, Tennessee.
Build Note: Frames the Coal Creek Wars: growing coal output and the value of mine labor explain why the state's convict-leasing of prisoners to replace free miners provoked armed resistance in Anderson County.

Standard Text: Describe how the Great Depression and New Deal programs impacted Tennesseans, including the significance of: the Agricultural Adjustment Act, Civilian Conservation Corps, Tennessee Valley Authority, and Great Smoky Mountains National Park.
Chart Title: The TVA and Rural Electrification of Tennessee, 1930s-1950s
What the Chart Shows: Line chart showing the rising share of Tennessee farms with electric power from the early 1930s through the 1950s after the TVA's creation.
Data Source: TVA power program statistics and U.S. Census of Agriculture, percentage of Tennessee farms with electricity (or TVA electric customers served), 1930s-1950s
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government / wholly owned U.S. government corporation)
Citation: Tennessee Valley Authority historical/annual reports; U.S. Census of Agriculture, Tennessee farms reporting electricity, 1930-1954.
Build Note: Directly supports the TVA portion of the New Deal standard; the steep rise from single-digit farm electrification to near-universal service dramatizes the agency's impact on rural life.

Standard Text: Evaluate Tennessee’s contributions during World War II, including the impact of Camp Forrest, Camp Tyson, and Oak Ridge as well as the influence of Tennesseans during the war (e.g., Cornelia Fort and Cordell Hull).
Chart Title: The Secret City: Oak Ridge Population, 1943-1945
What the Chart Shows: Line chart showing Oak Ridge growing from open farmland to one of Tennessee's largest cities within about two years during World War II.
Data Source: Manhattan District History and U.S. government records, Oak Ridge (Clinton Engineer Works) resident population, 1943-1945
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Army, Manhattan District History (Office of Scientific and Technical Information/DOE OpenNet); U.S. Census Bureau population data for Oak Ridge, TN.
Build Note: Quantifies the scale of Tennessee's WWII contribution; Oak Ridge's near-instant growth to roughly 75,000 residents makes the Manhattan Project's footprint tangible for students.

Standard Text: Describe major agricultural shifts in Tennessee post-World War II and their impact economically and socially.
Chart Title: The Farm Exodus: Number of Tennessee Farms, 1945-1974
What the Chart Shows: Line chart showing the sharp decline in the number of Tennessee farms in the decades after World War II.
Data Source: U.S. Census of Agriculture, number of farms in Tennessee, 1945, 1950, 1954, 1959, 1964, 1969, 1974
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Census Bureau / USDA, Census of Agriculture, Tennessee farm counts, 1945-1974.
Build Note: Documents the post-WWII agricultural shift the standard names: mechanization and consolidation cut farm numbers roughly in half, pushing rural Tennesseans toward cities and industry.

Standard Text: Describe major agricultural shifts in Tennessee post-World War II and their impact economically and socially.
Chart Title: Tennessee Urbanizes: Growth of the Four Major Cities, 1900-1980
What the Chart Shows: Multi-line chart tracing the twentieth-century population growth of Memphis, Nashville, Knoxville, and Chattanooga from 1900 to 1980.
Data Source: U.S. Census Bureau municipal population, 1900-1980, for Memphis, Nashville, Knoxville, and Chattanooga
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: Campbell Gibson, Population of the 100 Largest Cities and Other Urban Places in the United States: 1790 to 1990 (U.S. Census Bureau Working Paper No. 27, 1998).
Build Note: Pairs with the farm-exodus chart to show the rural-to-urban migration behind post-WWII social and economic change; students can compare the trajectories of the four grand-division cities.

Standard Text: Discuss the impact of major businesses in Tennessee, such as: AutoZone; Nissan; Eastman; Toyota; FedEx; Volkswagen; HCA
Chart Title: From Farm to Factory: Tennessee Manufacturing and Nonfarm Employment Growth
What the Chart Shows: Line chart showing long-run growth in Tennessee's total nonfarm and manufacturing employment.
Data Source: BLS Current Employment Statistics (State and Metro Area), Tennessee total nonfarm and manufacturing employment time series
Data Rights: Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government)
Citation: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics (State and Metro Area Employment), Tennessee.
Build Note: Contextualizes the standard's list of major employers (Nissan, FedEx, Eastman, Toyota, Volkswagen, AutoZone, HCA) by showing the industrial job base they built on; BLS series are official and public domain.
